textContent.text: When the breeze blows just right, that's the time to fly a kite! Kites are sheets of fabric or paper designed to catch the wind. There are many different kinds of kites, so there's one out there for everyone to enjoy.

pieces.text: Most kites have one string and are simple to fly. People enjoy watching these kites float calmly in the sky. The most familiar single-line kites are diamond-shaped. Their fabric is attached to a simple frame of two crossed sticks. Single-line kites may also be shaped like boxes or triangles. These shapes come from more complex frames. Other single-line kites, called
, are frameless. Parafoils take shape when the wind fills them with air.

textContent.text: Single-line kites are fun and easy to fly, but some people want something more active. Stunt kites usually have two strings, one for each hand. By pulling on the strings, stunt kite fliers make their kites dance, dive, and spin. There are even contests where individuals and teams perform tricks to music. Performers must be true athletes to control their kites.

For many people, the beauty of kites is not just in how they fly. Kites themselves have long been treated as works of art. Many traditional Chinese kites are designed to look like dragons with long, snakelike bodies. Others are painted with colorful flowers and animals. Similarly, in New Zealand, the Maori people are known for their bird-shaped kites adorned with shells and feathers. With these beautiful additions, kites can be admired whether they are in the sky or on the ground!

textContent.text: Fistball is sometimes described as "volleyball with a bounce." The two sports have a lot in common: two teams play on a court divided by a net. A team can hit the ball three times to get it over the net. And teams score when the other team fails to return a ball.

A key difference is that a fistball, but not a volleyball, may bounce on the ground once before a player hits it. Also, fistball players can only strike the ball with one arm or a closed fist. They cannot use the open-handed strike that volleyball players use. And a fistball team has only five, not six, players. They are spread out across a court that is six times larger than a volleyball court. That's a lot more ground to cover!

Fistball requires strength, speed, and endurance. Matches are played in up to five rounds that can each last ten minutes or more. Players dash, dive, and roll on the ground to hit the ball. The ball accelerates as it gets punched and bounced off the ground. It can reach speeds well over sixty miles per hour! Fistball certainly has enough fist-pumping action to thrill any sports fan.

textContent.text: Fistball is sometimes described as "volleyball with a bounce." The two sports have a lot in common: two teams play on a court divided by a net. A team can hit the ball three times to get it over the net. And teams score when the other team fails to return a ball.

A key difference is that a fistball, but not a volleyball, may bounce on the ground once before a player hits it. Also, fistball players can only strike the ball with one arm or a closed fist. They cannot use the open-handed strike that volleyball players use. And a fistball team has only five, not six, players. They are spread out across a court that is six times larger than a volleyball court. That's a lot more ground to cover!

textContent.text: Imagine taking a walk in the woods. Almost hidden at the base of a tree, a tiny door catches your eye. Crouching down to look closer, you see a whole tiny garden. It's a fairy garden! Fairy gardens are miniature gardens that look like homes for little magical creatures. They can be planted anywhere—at the base of a tree, in a small corner of a backyard, or in a container. They can be enjoyed inside or outside, anywhere with a small space in need of a little magic.

People who plant fairy gardens choose small-leaved plants like elfin thyme or fairy fern. A nine-inch-tall type of fig tree called "tiny limey" could be a towering tree in a fairy garden! A dollar-sized patch of green moss could be a vast lawn. But it's not enough to choose all tiny plants for a fairy garden; it's also important that they all require the same amounts of water and sunlight.

After planting, it's time to add some little fairy touches, like tiny figures or objects. Some fairy gardens are based on fairy tales. These might have little figures of fairies, animals, or well-known story characters. Fairy gardens may also have little houses, benches, or pebble pathways. Fancy ones might even have waterfalls or ponds. But some fairy gardens offer just a few hints of magical activity, like a tiny shovel or a small doorway. That way, people who stumble upon them are left to imagine what wee beings might live nearby.

textContent.text: Birds are all around us. They chatter outside our windows, fly through the skies, and nest in the trees. But how many people ever take a close look at these familiar feathered friends? Actually, millions of people observe wild birds as a hobby. Bird-watching, also known as birding, is a popular pastime that anyone can enjoy.

pieces.text: If you want to be a bird-watcher, first try using your ears. Birds are often easier to find by listening than by looking. An American robin, for example, announces itself with a cheerful

. The scratchy scream of a barn owl could give a clue to where it's hidden in the woods. And a house wren's bright, bubbly song sets it apart from the black-capped chickadee. You might hear that tiny bird singing
instead.

textContent.text: After locating a bird by sound, you may want to take a closer look. A pair of binoculars is a great birding tool to help zoom in on a bird. Another useful tool is a field guide that describes all the birds in your area. The pictures and information can help you know what birds you're seeing. Some bird-watchers also carry notebooks to record the different birds they find. They might even keep "life lists" of all the birds they've ever seen. There are about eighteen thousand kinds of birds in the world. That is certainly enough to keep any birder busy for a lifetime.

textContent.text: For thousands of years, people have enjoyed playing with marbles. But today, these toys are not just for fun and games. They have a long history, and they come in many shapes, sizes, and colors. For those reasons, many people enjoy collecting them, too.

The early marbles of ancient Egyptians, Romans, and Native Americans were handmade from materials like stone, wood, and clay. Today's marbles are mostly made out of glass by machines. There are many different colors and styles. "Clearies" are made of clear glass or colored glass that lets light shine through. Cat's-eyes have clear glass, too, with bands of color that can be seen inside. Other marbles are opaque. For instance, some marbles are made of materials like stone or light-blocking glass, which are not see-through.

Marble collectors try to find different kinds of marbles. Some collectors seek out rare or older types, such as handmade German marbles from the 1800s or American marbles produced in the mid-1900s. Others just collect as many pretty and interesting marbles as they can find.

contents.text: A relative pronoun introduces a dependent (or relative) clause that describes a noun or pronoun. The five main relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that.
The relative pronouns who and whom give information about people.

header.text: To figure out whether to use who or whom, restate the dependent clause with a personal pronoun. If the clause uses a subject pronoun (he, she, or they), use who. If the clause uses an object pronoun (him, her, or them), use whom.

sentences.text: The woman who lives next door grows tomatoes in her garden.
She lives next door.
Peter, whom you met yesterday, has four younger brothers.
You met him yesterday.

header.text: The relative pronoun that gives necessary information about things. Necessary information narrows down what you're talking about and is not set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to a park that has a tire swing.
The information narrows down which park we walked to. It is necessary.

header.text: The relative pronoun which adds unnecessary information about things. This extra information does not narrow down what you're talking about. It is always set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to Glendale Park, which has a tire swing.
The information is extra. It does not narrow down which park we walked to.

header.text: The relative pronoun whose shows possession.

contents.text: Emily, whose hair is quite long, likes wearing braids.

header.text: Do not confuse whose with who's. Who's is a contraction for who is or who has. It does not show possession.

sentences.text: Emily, who's quite tall, can reach the top shelf.
Emily, who is quite tall, can reach the top shelf.

header.text: The dependent clause gives information about a thing, the stuffed peppers. The information is necessary and is not set off by commas. So, use the relative pronoun that.

contents.text: Simon ate the stuffed peppers that Bryan prepared.

contents.text: A relative pronoun introduces a dependent (or relative) clause that describes a noun or pronoun. The five main relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that.
The relative pronouns who and whom give information about people.

header.text: To figure out whether to use who or whom, restate the dependent clause with a personal pronoun. If the clause uses a subject pronoun (he, she, or they), use who. If the clause uses an object pronoun (him, her, or them), use whom.

sentences.text: The woman who lives next door grows tomatoes in her garden.
She lives next door.
Peter, whom you met yesterday, has four younger brothers.
You met him yesterday.

header.text: The relative pronoun that gives necessary information about things. Necessary information narrows down what you're talking about and is not set off by commas.

sentences.text: We walked to a park that has a tire swing.
The information narrows down which park we walked to. It is necessary.

sentences.text: We walked to Glendale Park, which has a tire swing.
The information is extra. It does not narrow down which park we walked to.
